headline: Rates Edge Lower as Oil Slides; Fed Hike Still Set
tileReason: The daily 30-year average slipped to 7.46% Wednesday as oil prices fell and bonds firmed, even as Fed minutes showed almost all officials expect more rate hikes.
takeaway:
Rates eased a little again Wednesday. Mortgage News Daily's 30-year average slipped to 7.46% from 7.48% Tuesday, the second small dip in a row, though it is still about 0.20% higher than at the start of last week. Other trackers sit lower: Mortgage Research Center showed 7.30% and Zillow 7.23% Wednesday afternoon.

Falling oil prices helped bonds. U.S. crude fell about 3% Wednesday to its lowest close since late August after a big jump in U.S. oil stockpiles, which eases inflation worries. The 10-year Treasury yield, which mortgage rates tend to follow, closed near 5.07% Wednesday, down from 5.10% Tuesday, and mortgage bond prices rose a bit.

The Fed's meeting notes didn't change much. Minutes of the Fed's late-October meeting, released Wednesday afternoon, showed almost all officials expect more rate increases will be needed, and a couple said a bigger half-point step could be considered in December if inflation stays hot. Officials also flagged heavy borrowing tied to the AI building boom as a risk. Markets had largely expected this, and the minutes had little visible effect on mortgage rates.

This morning's news was mixed. Weekly jobless claims rose slightly to 203,000, a bit more than forecast, and a Philadelphia Fed survey showed factory activity in that region cooled sharply to 6.3 from 20.9, though the prices factories pay jumped. The 10-year yield is about 5.05% to 5.09% this morning, close to Wednesday's level, with several Fed officials speaking today.

A December hike still looks all but certain. Futures markets, where traders bet on the Fed's next move, put the odds of a quarter-point increase in the Fed's short-term rate on Dec 9 at about 91% to 96% this morning, with the rest on a bigger half-point move. These are market expectations, not a Fed forecast, and New York Fed President Williams has pushed back on going bigger.

Lenders still have some cushion. The Optimal Blue conforming index, which tracks rates on loans borrowers actually locked, sat about 2.19% above the 10-year Treasury on Nov 17, compared with a long-run average of about 1.76%. That extra room means lenders don't have to pass along every bit of a bond-market selloff.

The next tests come quickly. Freddie Mac's weekly rate survey comes out at 9 AM PT today, and the Fed's preferred inflation measure (PCE, a broad gauge of consumer prices) is due Nov 25, just before Thanksgiving. After that: the Dec 4 jobs report, the Dec 9 Fed decision and November consumer prices on Dec 10.

fedOdds.title: Odds of a Fed hike on Dec 9
fedOdds.source: CME FedWatch via Decrypt as reported by Trading and Investment News (Nov 19, 11:51 GMT); CME FedWatch via Seoul Economic Daily (Nov 19, 01:08 GMT); Trading Economics (Nov 19)
fedOdds.note: These are the odds of a quarter-point hike; the rest is on a half-point move, so a hike of some size is close to 100%. The latest CME FedWatch reading cited this morning is about 91% quarter-point and 9% half-point, up from about 6.5% for the bigger move a day earlier. An overnight reading after the Fed minutes showed 95.7% and 4.3%, so readings differ by source and time.
fedOdds.watch: The Nov 25 PCE inflation report and the Dec 4 jobs report could shift the odds between a quarter-point and a half-point hike.

drivers.title: Fed officials expect more hikes
drivers.text: Minutes of the Fed's October meeting showed almost all officials expect more rate increases, and a couple raised the idea of a bigger half-point step in December; Governor Waller said the same this week. When investors expect the Fed to keep raising its short-term rate, longer-term yields and mortgage rates have a hard time falling.

drivers.title: Inflation still running hot
drivers.text: October consumer prices beat forecasts for the third month in a row, wholesale prices are up 6.5% from a year ago, and factories in the Philadelphia Fed survey reported paying more this month. Bond investors demand higher yields when inflation eats into what their interest is worth, and mortgage rates follow.

drivers.title: Oil prices sliding
drivers.text: U.S. crude fell about 3% Wednesday to its lowest close since late August after a big build in stockpiles. Cheaper energy eases inflation worries, which helped Treasury yields and mortgage rates edge lower.

drivers.title: Signs of a cooling economy
drivers.text: Jobless claims ticked up to 203,000 this morning, more people are staying on unemployment longer, and the Philadelphia Fed's factory gauge dropped to its weakest in six months. Softer economic news tends to pull yields and mortgage rates down.

drivers.title: Mortgage rates still far above Treasuries
drivers.text: The Optimal Blue conforming index sat about 2.19% above the 10-year Treasury yield on Nov 17, compared with a long-run average of about 1.76%. That wide gap is a cushion: lenders can absorb part of a jump in Treasury yields without raising rates as much.

outlook.baseSource: Mortgage News Daily, Nov 18 close (latest available)
outlook.basis: The odds are close to even, with a slight lean higher. Mortgage rates eased to about 7.46% Wednesday, and the 10-year Treasury yield has slipped to around 5.07%-5.09%. Working against borrowers: a December Fed hike is close to fully expected, Fed minutes show almost all officials see more increases ahead, and inflation reports keep running hot. In borrowers' favor: oil prices have fallen to their lowest since late August, some job and factory data are softening, and mortgage rates still sit unusually far above the 10-year Treasury (about 2.19% vs. a long-run average near 1.76%). Big swing events: the Nov 25 report on the Fed's preferred inflation measure, the Dec 4 jobs report, the Dec 9 Fed decision, Dec 10 consumer prices and oil headlines tied to Iran.
outlook.caveat: This is professional judgment from 30+ years watching these markets, not a guarantee. One oil headline or data surprise can move rates a quarter point in a day.

talkingPoints.buyers: The daily 30-year average eased to 7.46% Wednesday, still near its highest in over a month but below the 7.6%-plus levels of early October. Fed officials expect to keep raising their short-term rate, so the next few weeks could be bumpy. If you're under contract or close to it, talk with Stuart about how locking, a float-down option (which lets you take a lower rate if rates drop after you lock), or waiting would each fit your closing date.
talkingPoints.sellers: Rates are holding near 7.5%, and mortgage applications fell last week as rates climbed, so buyers are feeling the pinch. Realistic pricing, or a seller credit buyers can use to lower their rate, can help a home stand out heading into the holidays.
talkingPoints.oneLiner: Mortgage rates eased slightly to about 7.46% as oil prices fell, but Fed minutes show more rate hikes are likely on the way.
